/ceske-velkoprevorstvi/.title: Grand Priory of Bohemia
/ceske-velkoprevorstvi/.description: The Grand Priory of Bohemia of the Sovereign Order of Malta: its seat in Prague's Lesser Town, history, officers and palace.
/ceske-velkoprevorstvi/.body:
The Grand Priory of Bohemia is one of the Grand Priories of the Sovereign Order of Malta. The Order has been present in Prague's Lesser Town (Malá Strana) since the second half of the 12th century, when Duke Vladislaus II gave the Knights of St John land at the foot of the Judith Bridge; the Prague commandery is the oldest surviving precinct of the Order in the world. After its suppression by the Communists, the Grand Priory survived in exile. Its work in Prague was officially restored on 1 April 1990 and publicly announced on 20 April 1990 at Mass in the Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain, on the eve of Pope John Paul II's first visit to the Czech lands.

The seat of the Grand Priory is the Grand Prior's Palace on Velkopřevorské náměstí. Its church is the Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain in Lázeňská street.

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-ceskeho-v.title: History of the Grand Priory of Bohemia
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-ceskeho-v.description: From the 12th-century commandery at the Judith Bridge to the restoration of the Grand Priory in 1990.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-ceskeho-v.body:
The Order of St John was brought to Bohemia by Duke Vladislaus II, who had come to know its work while taking part in the Second Crusade in the army of the German King Conrad III. Some time between 1158 and 1169 (according to the latest research, more probably around 1169) the Knights of St John received land south of the bishop's court at the bridgehead of the Judith Bridge. The centre of the Order became the church of the Mother of God beneath the Chain; the name recalls either the chain that closed the gate of the commandery or the chain stretched across the river to stop boats and rafts so that tolls could be collected.

Further commanderies were founded over time, the most important at Strakonice, Horažďovice, Manětín and Český Dub. In 1301 Pope Boniface VIII granted the prior of Our Lady beneath the Chain the right to pontificals. In 1378 the body of the late Emperor Charles IV lay in state for a day and a night in the Order's church in Prague. In 1393 the neutral ground of the Order witnessed the ugly scenes in which King Wenceslas IV attacked the Archbishop of Prague, John of Jenštejn; the victim of the king's anger was ultimately the vicar general, John of Nepomuk.

In 1402 the Order became the owner of the whole of Strakonice Castle, which after the Hussites drove the Order from Prague became its refuge and its centre in Bohemia. The priors general there were zealous defenders of the Catholic faith and leading members of the Strakonice and Zelená Hora leagues opposed to King George of Poděbrady. In 1512 Pope Julius II granted the priors of Strakonice the right to pontificals until the Prague convent should be restored. Czech knights also took part, if only in symbolic numbers, in the heroic defence of Malta (1565) and the Battle of Lepanto (1571).

On the eve of the Thirty Years' War the Spanish Carmelite Dominic of Jesus and Mary found at Strakonice a painting of the Virgin and Child that had been desecrated by Protestant soldiers; he carried it before the troops at the Battle of the White Mountain. As the victory was attributed to the Virgin's help, the image came to be venerated as Our Lady of Victory. From 1626 the head of the Order in Bohemia bore the title of Grand Prior; among them, Rudolf Colloredo-Wallsee won fame in 1648 for his heroic defence of Prague against the Swedes.

In 1694 the convent returned with the Grand Prior from Strakonice to Prague, where on 22 February 1718 one of the miracles required for the canonisation of John of Nepomuk took place (the rescue of seven-year-old Rosalie Hodánková from under the ice). The residence of the Grand Priors of Prague was built in 1726–1727, and the convent on the other side of the church in 1728–1731. In 1784 the Order was entrusted with the spiritual care of the Church of Our Lady of Victory with its world-famous Infant Jesus of Prague. The Grand Priory of Bohemia, including its convent of priests, was the only one to withstand the general collapse of the Order's structures in the upheavals of the Napoleonic wars and the secularisation of Europe. Grand Prior Othenio Lichnowsky-Werdenberg brought the Order renown by establishing eight hospital trains for the wounded of the First World War; together they covered 1,062,760 km and carried 359,945 wounded from the front. The Order's doctors performed 27,163 operations during the war, more than half of them in the Order's field hospitals. The Grand Priory also financed the building and running of the hospice at Tantur in the Holy Land.

On 2 April 1881 Emperor Francis Joseph I raised the Grand Prior of Bohemia and Austria (and his successors) to the rank of Austrian Prince. After the fall of the monarchy, land reform, the economic crisis and the political climate diminished the Order's property. For political reasons the Grand Priory was divided in 1938 into the Grand Priory of Bohemia and the Grand Priory of Austria. Two figures helped the Order through the difficult years of the Second World War: Karel Cardinal Kašpar, Prince-Archbishop of Prague and Primate of Bohemia, and Karel Prince of Schwarzenberg, who also ensured the survival of the Grand Priory in exile after the Communists suppressed the Order in 1950. The Order's work in Prague was officially restored on 1 April 1990; the restoration was publicly announced on 20 April 1990 at Mass in the Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain, on the eve of Pope John Paul II's visit to Prague.

PhDr. Milan Buben, Ph.D.,
Knight of Magistral Grace

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-ceskeho-v.title: Heads of the Grand Priory of Bohemia
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-ceskeho-v.description: Preceptors, masters, priors general, grand priors and their deputies in Bohemia since the 12th century.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-ceskeho-v.body:
The title of the head of the Order in the Czech lands

The title of the head of the Order in the Czech lands has changed over time. At first the heads of the Order were called preceptors, later masters and priors general. Beginning with Wilhelm Zdenko Count Wratislaw of Mitrowitz (head of the Order in the Czech lands 1626–1637) they have been called Grand Priors. In 1881 Emperor Francis Joseph I raised the Grand Prior of Bohemia to the rank of Prince, creating the unique title of Prince Grand Prior, with the style "Serene Highness" from 1905. When the office of Grand Prior is vacant, or the elected Grand Prior cannot exercise it, the Grand Priory is led by a lieutenant, a regent or a procurator.

/velkoprevorsky-palac/.title: Grand Prior's Palace
/velkoprevorsky-palac/.description: The Baroque Grand Prior's Palace in Prague's Lesser Town, seat of the Grand Priory of Bohemia: history, architecture and use today.
/velkoprevorsky-palac/.body:
The Grand Prior's Palace in Prague's Lesser Town is the seat of the Grand Priory of Bohemia. It stands on the site of the commandery of the Knights of St John, founded here in the second half of the 12th century beside the Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain; the present palace still follows the ground plan of its three-winged Romanesque hospital.

The Baroque building

The rebuilding was decided by Grand Prior Karl Leopold Count Herberstein. The plans were drawn up by the Milanese builder Giuseppe Bartolomeo Scotti, and the palace was built in 1726–1727 and completed under Grand Prior Gundaker Poppo Count Dietrichstein: a single-storey, four-winged residence with dormers and oval windows.

Both portals, on the south and west sides, come from the workshop of Matthias Bernhard Braun and bear the arms of Grand Prior Dietrichstein. The same workshop decorated the monumental three-flight staircase with putti bearing lights, one of the finest in the Czech lands. The interiors retain stucco ceilings, inlaid doors, parquet floors, marble fireplaces and tiled stoves from the Dietrichstein manufactory. At the corner on Velkopřevorské náměstí stands a 190 cm kerbstone, probably the largest in Prague.

Around 1730 Grand Prior Dietrichstein ordered six tapestries from the Brussels workshop of Peter van den Hecke for the main hall, now called the Knights' Hall. They were taken away during the Nazi occupation; four were found after the war and are today on permanent loan from the Grand Priory of Bohemia at the seat of the Order in Rome.

In the 20th century

After the land reform the Order let the palace in 1919–1931 to the legation of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (later Yugoslavia). During the occupation the property was transferred to the German Reich, and in 1949 the Communists seized the palace; from 1950 it housed the Music Museum of the National Museum. In 1984 scenes of Miloš Forman's film Amadeus were shot here.

Under Act No. 338/1991 the palace was returned to the Order; the museum moved out in 2003. In the floods of August 2002 water filled the cellars and the ground floor. In 2019–2022 the roof structure, attacked by dry rot, was restored and newly covered.

Today

The palace serves the Order and hosts public lectures and conferences. Its garden lies behind the so-called Lennon Wall. The state rooms can be hired; details and contacts for organisers are on the palace's website www.velkoprevorskypalac.eu.

Source: Milan M. Buben, Chrám Panny Marie pod řetězem a Velkopřevorský palác. Dějiny a průvodce (The Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain and the Grand Prior's Palace: History and Guide), Prague 2026.

/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.title: Activities of the Order of Malta in the Czech Republic
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.description: Care for the elderly and people in need, schools, the pilgrimage to Lourdes, land and forests, youth and cathedral service.
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.body: The Order of Malta is active in the Czech Republic in many fields. Most of its services are provided today by organisations founded by the Grand Priory of Bohemia, each with its own management and its own website.

/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.title: Help for the elderly
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.description: Maltézská pomoc, founded by the Grand Priory in 2002, provides personal assistance and volunteer support for the elderly.
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.body:
The Knights of Malta have always helped people in need, the weak and the sick. Today many people of advanced age find themselves in difficulty. It is not only their health: sometimes they need help in ordinary daily situations, or they suffer from loneliness and would simply like someone to talk to.

That is why in 2002 we founded the public-benefit company Maltézská pomoc, which provides a wide range of help for the elderly. In twelve centres across the Czech Republic we offer professional personal assistance and coordinate hundreds of volunteers, whose work makes life easier for many elderly people.

Would you like to know more, help or get involved in our work for the elderly? Visit the Maltézská pomoc website (in Czech) for all the details.

/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.title: Help for people in need
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.description: Support for people with disabilities, families in hardship and the homeless.
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.body:
In every period of our history there have been people who fell into hardship through no fault of their own and found themselves on the margins of society. The seriously ill, the poor, victims of war: for centuries they could count on finding a refuge with us and support in returning to life. Helping those in need has always been at the heart of the Order of Malta's work.

We see supporting people on the margins of society as our task today as well. Our help goes above all to people with disabilities, to families in difficult social and economic circumstances and to the homeless. We help them with their basic needs and support them, wherever possible, in caring for themselves and their families.

Would you like to know where and how we help? See our current projects on the websites of Maltézská pomoc and Česká maltézská pomoc České Budějovice (in Czech).

/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.title: Schools
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.description: Schools founded by the Grand Priory of Bohemia: a nursing college in Prague, a primary school in Kladno and a grammar school in Skuteč.
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.body:
The Order of Malta has always been devoted above all to running hospitals and helping those in need. These values are reflected in education too: the Grand Priory of Bohemia is the founder of three schools, which train future nurses and bring up the young generation in the spirit of Christian tradition. The schools' websites are in Czech.

Nursing College of the Sovereign Order of Malta

Diploma programme in general nursing, full-time and part-time. Since September 2026 the college has been in a new building in Žerotínova street (formerly in Ječná street).

Žerotínova 1143/38, 130 00 Prague 3
vos.mojezdravka.cz · Facebook

Knights of Malta Primary School

Primary school for grades 1 to 9, with an after-school club and a school club.

Školská 349, 272 01 Kladno
www.zsmr.cz

Grammar school with a school club, a boarding house and a school canteen.

/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.title: Pilgrimage to Lourdes
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.description: The Order's annual pilgrimage to Lourdes with sick pilgrims, their medical staff and volunteers.
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.body: Every year we help sick and healthy pilgrims who long to see one of the world's most important places of pilgrimage with their own eyes: Lourdes. Above all we bring seriously ill people, most often wheelchair users, to the place of miracles and healing. They are accompanied by our professional medical staff and volunteers, and healthy people can join too, combining a spiritual experience with helping others. Details are on the website of the Order's pilgrimage (in Czech).

/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.title: Care for land and forests
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.description: The Grand Priory looks after 600 hectares of forest using close-to-nature selective management.
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.body:
Since the Middle Ages the Order administered extensive lands in Bohemia and Moravia. On the territory of today's Czech Republic the Order of Malta historically owned commanderies, in effect large estates farmed by the knights of the Order, and it also looked after villages in which it built up farming. This founded our tradition of caring for land and forests, above all managing them well in a sustainable way over the long term.

Today we look after 600 hectares of forest in Silesia and south-west Bohemia. In our forests we practise the time-tested selective cutting method, which is close to nature, supports the diversity of species and ages in the forest and so limits damage and clear-cut areas. Put simply, a forest managed this way resembles an original primeval forest, with the difference that old trees are not left to fall and rot but are felled individually in good time. We treat farmland with the same care: we lease it on long terms to local farmers and make sure its fertility is preserved.

/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.title: Other activities
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.description: Masses and concerts in the Order's church, the Czech Maltese Youth and the Maltese cathedral service.
/cinnosti-maltezskeho-radu-v-ceske-repub.body:
In our ancient church Holy Mass is celebrated at least twice a week, and the well-attended concert series Organ Vespers of the Knights of Malta takes place there under the auspices of Prague 1 Municipal District.

The Czech Maltese Youth is also very active, organising leisure and other charitable activities above all for young people with disabilities and others in need.

The Maltese cathedral service looks after pilgrims and worshippers not only in Prague Cathedral but also at other major church events.

/radovy-kostel-panny-marie-pod-retezem/.title: Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain
/radovy-kostel-panny-marie-pod-retezem/.description: The Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain in Prague's Lesser Town, church of the Grand Priory of Bohemia: history, services and concerts.
/radovy-kostel-panny-marie-pod-retezem/.body: The Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain in Lázeňská street is the church of the Grand Priory of Bohemia, at the heart of the oldest surviving precinct of the Order of Malta in the world.

/radovy-kostel-panny-marie-pod-retezem/o.title: About the church
/radovy-kostel-panny-marie-pod-retezem/o.description: The Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain: building history, altars, chapels and works of art.
/radovy-kostel-panny-marie-pod-retezem/o.body:
The Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain stands at the heart of the oldest surviving precinct of the Order in the world. In the second half of the 12th century the Knights of St John built a three-aisled Romanesque basilica here at the foot of the Judith Bridge; its existence is confirmed by a charter of Pope Lucius III dated 23 October 1182. The name "beneath the Chain" is explained either by the chain that closed the gate of the commandery or the bridge at night, or by a chain stretched across the river when tolls were collected.

The building

Gothic rebuilding probably began in the first half of the 14th century: two towers and the choir were built, but the nave was never completed. Today's church is therefore only the choir of the planned Gothic church. The space between the towers and the church is a courtyard where the Order's cemetery once lay, and the arcades of the Romanesque basilica can still be seen on the north wall of the palace. The Gothic porch between the towers dates from around 1400.

After its devastation by the Hussites in 1420 and a fire in 1503 the church was repeatedly restored, and in 1591–1611 it was remodelled in the Renaissance style. It received its early Baroque appearance under Grand Prior Rudolf Count Colloredo-Wallsee: work began in 1645 and, after an interruption caused by the Swedish occupation of the Lesser Town, was completed in 1654–1655 by the builders Santino de Bossi and Carlo Lurago. The vaults are decorated with stucco by Italian stuccoists.

Altars and works of art

The high altar, completed in 1741, holds an altarpiece by Karel Škréta from around 1651. It shows knights of the Order with their Grand Master, above whom the Virgin and Child and St John the Baptist appear. The fortified tower in the background shows that the scene is the defence of Malta in 1565, not the Battle of Lepanto, as is often said. The sculptures of the high altar and the angels on either side are probably the work of Jan Petr Wenda, whose workshop also made the pulpit.

The church has ten altars. In the chapel of St John of Nepomuk, where according to tradition the saint was seized in 1393, fragments of Gothic frescoes from the second half of the 13th century survive. The chapel of St John the Baptist, patron of the Order, has an altarpiece by Anton Stevens von Steinfels from 1660. The oldest painting in the church, from the end of the 16th century, shows the nursing Mother of God with St Anne and the young St John the Baptist. The chapel of St Barbara holds a late work by Karel Škréta, the Beheading of St Barbara (1671–1674).

Also notable are the marble statue of Grand Prior Rudolf Colloredo-Wallsee by Emanuel Max, set up in the church in 1857, the stained-glass windows of the sanctuary from 1850 and the Baroque organ case of 1720. The church is rich in heraldry and in tombstones of the Order's dignitaries and benefactors; the oldest belongs to Prior Peter, to whom Pope Boniface IX granted the right to pontificals in 1395.

Today

Since 2004 the church has been the Order's church, with a rector. Regular services are celebrated here and concerts of sacred and classical music are held. The entrance is from Lázeňská street through the gate between the towers.

Source: Milan M. Buben, Chrám Panny Marie pod řetězem a Velkopřevorský palác. Dějiny a průvodce (The Church of Our Lady beneath the Chain and the Grand Prior's Palace: History and Guide), Prague 2026.

/ochrana-osobnich-udaju/.body:
This website uses no analytics or advertising cookies and does not track visitors. Fonts and images are loaded from this website itself.

The home pages and the calendar pages show a calendar from the AddCal service (addcal.co). When it loads, your browser sends AddCal the technical data needed to display it (IP address and browser details). You can also view the calendar directly at addcal.co/c/calendarGPB.

The controller of personal data is the Grand Priory of Bohemia, Velkopřevorské náměstí 4, 118 00 Prague 1. Please send questions about data protection to gpb@smom.cz.

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/.title: The Order of Malta
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/.description: The Sovereign Order of Malta: its mission, spirituality, history, Grand Master and diplomatic relations.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/.body:
The Sovereign Order of Malta is a lay religious order of the Catholic Church and a sovereign subject of international law. Since the 11th century it has served the sick and the poor and borne witness to the faith. The pages below introduce the Order; the Grand Magistry in Rome publishes its official texts on orderofmalta.int.

Official texts of the Grand Magistry

  • Mission
  • Spiritual commitment
  • History
  • The Grand Master
  • Frequently asked questions

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/o-radu/.title: About the Order
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/o-radu/.description: The Sovereign Order of Malta: one of the oldest institutions of Christian civilisation, present in the Czech lands since the 12th century.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/o-radu/.body:
The Sovereign Military Hospitaller Order of St. John of Jerusalem of Rhodes and of Malta is one of the oldest Catholic orders and therefore one of the longest-serving institutions of Christian civilisation. Its aim is to help all those in need, without distinction. Traditionally the Order concentrated above all on running hospitals, which is why its members are also called Hospitallers; the name Knights of St. John is used as well. The name Knights of Malta goes back to the 16th century, when the Order received the island of Malta in the Mediterranean.

The Order was founded in Jerusalem in the 11th century and has fulfilled its mission without interruption for more than 900 years. It is subject to no state or international organisation, and its independence gives it a unique diplomatic position in international conflicts and in bringing help quickly to crises anywhere in the world. The seat of the Order has been in Rome since 1834.

The Order has been present in the Czech lands without interruption since the 12th century. Historically it owned land, estates, villages and whole towns in Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia (Strakonice, for example). It has always concentrated on giving effective help to those in need. During the First World War and for several years afterwards, for instance, it ran hospital trains that cared for wounded soldiers: eight such trains travelled more than a million kilometres during the war and carried hundreds of thousands of wounded and sick.

Today the Order's work in the Czech Republic centres on the elderly, people with disabilities and others in need. It relies on a wide network of professionals and volunteers in the centres of Maltézská pomoc, o.p.s. and in Česká maltézská pomoc České Budějovice, o.p.s.

The Grand Priory of Bohemia is one of the Order's six Grand Priories; the others are those of Rome, of Lombardy and Venice, of Naples and Sicily, of England and of Austria. Alongside them, the Order has national associations in many countries on five continents.

Detailed information about the Order, its work and its history is published on the Order's international website, available in English, Italian, French, German and Spanish.

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/radova-spiritualit.title: Spirituality of the Order
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/radova-spiritualit.description: The Order of Malta as a lay religious order: vows, the Cardinal Patronus, the Prelate and the vocation of the Hospitaller.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/radova-spiritualit.body:
The Hospitaller Brothers of St. John of Jerusalem were recognised as a religious order by Pope Paschal II in 1113. As a religious order they are linked to the Holy See, while at the same time acting as an independent subject of international law.

In this respect the religious character of the Order coexists with its full sovereignty. The Grand Master is the head of a sovereign entity and at the same time the highest superior of the religious community of the Order. In this second role the Roman Catholic Church accords him the rank of a Cardinal.

Under canon law the Order of Malta is a lay religious order. Some of its members are religious (professed knights) who have taken the three vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. A second group has made a promise of obedience (knights in obedience), while most knights and dames are lay members. The Grand Master is elected from among the professed knights in perpetual vows. The eight points of the Maltese cross symbolise the eight Beatitudes and so point clearly to the spiritual mission of the Order. Under the Constitution, members of the Order are bound to lead an exemplary Christian life in private and in public, so as to keep alive the heritage and traditions of the Order of Malta.

Under the Constitution the Pope appoints a Cardinal as his representative to the Order. He bears the title of Cardinal Patronus; his task is to care for the spiritual life of the Order and its members and for its relations with the Holy See. The Pope also appoints the Prelate of the Order, choosing him from three candidates proposed by the Grand Master.

The Prelate is the religious superior of the Order's chaplains. The Order remains faithful to its essential mission: defending the faith and serving the suffering. Its members share the same vocation and work together for solidarity, justice and peace, on the basis of the teaching of the Gospel and in the closest union with the Holy See. They are engaged in active and dynamic charitable work sustained by prayer. No one becomes a knight or a dame for privileges of birth or for merit, but by answering an inner call to serve wherever there is material or moral need, wherever there is suffering.

Wherever the Hospitaller knights settled, they first built a hospital and a hostel for pilgrims, and only then, when it was necessary, fortifications. What does it mean to be a Hospitaller in the third millennium? It means giving oneself to relieving suffering and bringing the balm of Christian love and help to the sick anywhere in the world, not only in hospitals but also in their homes, in care homes and in shelters for the homeless. The Order devotes itself not only to the sick but also to the socially isolated, to victims of persecution and to refugees, regardless of race or creed.

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-radu-ve-s.title: History of the Order
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-radu-ve-s.description: From the hospital in Jerusalem through Cyprus, Rhodes and Malta to Rome: nine centuries of the Order of Malta.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-radu-ve-s.body:
1048 Jerusalem

The foundation of the Order of St. John dates from about 1048. At that time merchants from the ancient maritime republic of Amalfi obtained from the Caliph of Egypt permission to build a church, a convent and a hospital in Jerusalem, where pilgrims of any race or creed would be cared for.

The Order of St. John of Jerusalem, the monastic community that ran the hospital, became independent under its founder, Blessed Gerard. Pope Paschal II approved the foundation of the hospital with a papal bull of 15 February 1113. In the same bull he placed it under the protection of the Church and granted the Order the right to elect its superior without interference from any lay or religious authority. Through the bull the hospital community became a lay religious order. Its knights were religious who had taken the three monastic vows of poverty, chastity and obedience.

After the foundation of the Kingdom of Jerusalem the Order also took on the military defence of the sick and the pilgrims and the protection of its hospitals and of the kingdom's main roads. Alongside its hospital mission it thus took on the defence of the faith and of pilgrims. In this period the Order began to use the white eight-pointed cross that remains its symbol today.

1291 Cyprus

After the fall of Acre in 1291 and the loss of the Holy Land, the Order of St. John moved its seat and its hospital to Limassol on Cyprus, where it had been present since 1210 and held important property, privileges and trading rights.

Here too, faithful to its hospitaller tradition, it founded many new hospitals. Making use of the island's strategic position, it built up a large fleet that protected pilgrims sailing to the Holy Land. New knights joined in growing numbers, and the Order grew stronger. It acquired new lands and rights on Cyprus, above all along the coast; among the most important were the port of Famagusta, the city of Nicosia and many commanderies.

Growing instability on Cyprus limited the Order's expansion there, and the knights came to see Rhodes as a better base, to which they eventually moved. Lieutenants stayed on Cyprus to administer the priory and its commanderies (more than 60 in 1374) for another century, until the knights were withdrawn to the main convent on Rhodes in the mid-15th century.

1310 Rhodes

In 1307 a fleet carrying the knights of St. John under Grand Master Fra’ Foulques de Villaret landed on Rhodes. After taking full possession of the island in 1310, the knights moved their headquarters there. The island offered excellent natural harbours and held a strategic position between the Christian and the Muslim worlds. Defending Christendom required great naval strength, so the Order built a powerful fleet that sailed the eastern Mediterranean and won many famous battles.

By papal decree the Order gained independence and the right to maintain its own armed forces and to appoint ambassadors, which laid the foundations of its international sovereignty. From the early 14th century the Order's institutions and the knights who came to Rhodes were grouped by their native tongues. At first there were seven Tongues: Provence, Auvergne, France, Italy, Aragon (Navarre), England (with Scotland and Ireland) and Germany (which also included, among others, the Czech lands); an eighth, Castile and Portugal, was added later. Each Tongue had its priories or grand priories, bailiwicks and commanderies.

The Order was governed by the Grand Master (the Prince of Rhodes) with his Council. It minted its own coins and maintained diplomatic relations with other states. The high offices of the Order were given to representatives of the different Tongues, and its seat, the Convent, was made up of religious of many nations.

In 1523, after a six-month siege and hard fighting against the fleet and army of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, the knights were forced to surrender and left Rhodes with military honours.

1530 Malta

After the loss of Rhodes the Order had no territory of its own for several years. In 1530 Emperor Charles V granted it the island of Malta in fief. Once Pope Clement VII had approved the grant, a fleet carrying the knights under Grand Master Fra’ Philippe de Villiers de l’Isle Adam landed on Malta and formally took possession of the island. In return the Order undertook to remain neutral in conflicts between Christian states.

In 1565 the Ottomans laid siege to Malta. The Great Siege lasted three months; the knights, led by Grand Master Fra’ Jean de la Vallette, held out. A great period of building followed the victory. A new city and a new harbour were founded, the city named Valletta after its founder. Palaces, churches and a vast new system of fortifications were built, and patronage of the arts and architecture flourished. A great new hospital, one of the best organised and most effective of its time, was founded on the island; the Order established a school of anatomy and soon afterwards a faculty of medicine, and made notable contributions above all to ophthalmology and pharmacology. At the same time the Order kept up its military role: for centuries its fleet took part in many battles in the Mediterranean, above all against the Ottoman fleet and pirates.

1571 Battle of Lepanto

The Order's fleet took part in the naval battle of Lepanto, contributing to the victory of the united fleet of the Christian states and halting the Ottoman advance into Europe.

1798 Exile

In 1798, during his Egyptian campaign, Napoleon occupied Malta for its strategic position. Because the Order's rule forbade the knights to take up arms against other Christians, they were forced to leave the island. The Treaty of Amiens of 1802, under which the Order's rule over Malta was to be restored, was never put into effect.

1834 Rome

After temporary seats in Messina, Catania and Ferrara, the Order settled permanently in Rome in 1834. There it owns the Magistral Palace and, on the Aventine Hill, the Magistral Villa, both of which enjoy extraterritorial status and privileges.

The 20th and 21st centuries

From the second half of the 19th century the Order's main mission once again became hospitaller work. Over the past century it has grown and spread around the world, above all through the efforts of the grand priories and national associations. The Order intensified its hospitaller and charitable work during the First and especially the Second World War, under Grand Master Fra’ Ludovico Chigi Albani della Rovere (1931–1951).

The expansion of the Order's work as we know it today came under Grand Masters Fra’ Angelo de Mojana di Cologna (1962–1988) and Fra’ Andrew Bertie (1988–2008). The Order's present work around the world is described on orderofmalta.int.

Watch a video on the history and work of the Order (YouTube)

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-radu-ve-s.title: 1113: papal recognition
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-radu-ve-s.description: The bull Pie Postulatio Voluntatis of 15 February 1113, by which Pope Paschal II recognised the Hospitallers of St. John.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-radu-ve-s.body:
In February 2013, and throughout that year, the Sovereign Order of Malta celebrated a major anniversary: exactly 900 years earlier Pope Paschal II had issued the bull that officially recognised the religious community of the Hospitallers of St. John of Jerusalem.

This document, known from its opening words as the bull Pie Postulatio Voluntatis, laid the legal foundation for the sovereignty and independence of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, today the Sovereign Order of Malta, and was fundamental to its development.

The Order had been founded in the Holy Land more than half a century earlier as a monastic community caring for poor pilgrims in a hospital in Jerusalem. Through the bull the Hospitallers became a lay religious order.

The document is also of great institutional importance: in it the Pope granted the Order the absolute right to secure the continuation of its work by electing, on its own, the successors of its founder, Brother Gerard.

The bull, now kept in the National Library of Malta, still gives a clear picture of the role and importance of Blessed Gerard, of his personal holiness and of the group of distinguished religious who worked with him. It also stresses the importance of the services offered to pilgrims and the poor in Jerusalem.

The list of hospitals and hospices in France and Italy named in the bull, which existed only a few decades after the community was founded, shows that the institution founded by Brother Gerard was not confined to the Kingdom of Jerusalem but had already spread into Europe.

During 2013 the institutions of the Order on five continents marked the anniversary with many events. The most important was the gathering in Rome on 9 February 2013, when Cardinal Secretary of State Tarcisio Bertone celebrated Mass in St. Peter’s Basilica. Afterwards Pope Benedict XVI addressed more than 5,000 members and volunteers of the Order who had come from all over the world.

Watch the recording (YouTube)

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-radu-ve-s.title: The five Orders of St. John
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-radu-ve-s.description: The Sovereign Order of Malta and the four Orders of St. John recognised by it, united in the Alliance of the Orders of St. John.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/historie-radu-ve-s.body:
Besides the Sovereign Order of Malta there are four other Orders of St. John recognised as orders of chivalry.

They differ from other national orders in being founded on the Christian faith and in their tradition as lay Christian orders. The four Orders of St. John of Jerusalem are joined in the Alliance of the Orders of St. John and share with the Sovereign Order of Malta the same historical tradition and the same mission: helping the sick and the poor.

These orders are recognised by the sovereign authorities of the countries in which they are based. Below is a short description of the four Orders of St. John recognised by the Sovereign Order of Malta.

The Bailiwick of Brandenburg of the Order of St. John

The Order of St. John settled in Germany in the 12th and 13th centuries and founded a grand priory there. In the 16th century part of that grand priory, the Bailiwick of Brandenburg (a bailiwick is a territorial unit of the Order), became Protestant and remained under the protection of the Margraves of Brandenburg, later Kings of Prussia.

The bailiwick kept up friendly relations with the Sovereign Order of Malta. In 1811, however, it was suppressed by the King of Prussia, who later founded the Royal Prussian Order of St. John as an order of merit. In 1852 the order took back the name of the Bailiwick of Brandenburg.

In 1918, after the fall of the monarchy, it was separated from the state and became independent. Today it is present in a number of European countries, in Canada and in the United States. In Germany it runs or works with hospitals and homes for the elderly and runs an important emergency service, the Johanniter-Unfall-Hilfe. It also has independent branches in Finland, France, Hungary and Switzerland.

www.johanniter.org

The Order of St. John in the Netherlands

The Order of St. John spread to the Netherlands in the 12th century. A decisive year was 1811, when the King of Prussia suppressed the Bailiwick of Brandenburg.

In 1852 a number of its Dutch members came together to refound it. In 1909 ties were established with the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and in 1946 the group separated from the German order and was attached to the Dutch Crown, though not as an order of state.

Today the order runs hospitals and hospices and works with the Sovereign Order of Malta in various charitable activities.

www.johanniter.nl

The Order of St. John in Sweden

The Order settled in Scandinavia in the 12th century and became Protestant in 1530.

The new Order of St. John originally belonged to the Bailiwick of Brandenburg. In 1920 it was reorganised, still dependent on the German order but now under the protection of the Swedish Crown.

It became independent of Germany in 1946. Today it provides care for the elderly and the sick and works with Swedish hospitals, charities and Christian communities. It also takes part in international work for refugees and political prisoners.

www.johanniterorden.se

The Most Venerable Order of St. John of Jerusalem

The Order of St. John settled in the British Isles in the 12th century and, apart from a short period under Queen Mary, ceased to exist there under King Henry VIII.

The Venerable Order arose after an unsuccessful attempt to restore the Order of St. John in Britain in 1830. It was established as a humanitarian foundation only in 1870. In 1888 Queen Victoria recognised it, not as an order of state but as an order of the Crown.

Today it is well known for its ambulance services in many countries, for its eye hospital in Jerusalem and for first aid and nursing care. The Venerable Order has priories and associations in some 40 countries, most of them English-speaking.

It is the only one of the Orders of St. John that sets no religious requirement for admission.

www.orderofstjohn.org

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/stare-jazyky-radu/.title: The ancient Tongues of the Order
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/stare-jazyky-radu/.description: How the knights on Rhodes and Malta were grouped into Tongues, and how the national associations succeeded them.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/stare-jazyky-radu/.body:
At the beginning of the 14th century, with the acquisition of Rhodes and other islands of the archipelago, the Order of St. John took on the features of a state. Its government, led by the Grand Master and the Council, issued its own coinage and maintained diplomatic relations with other states.

New knights came to Rhodes from all over Europe, and it was natural for them to join those who spoke the same language and shared the same traditions.

The Chapter General of the Order, meeting in Montpellier in 1319, decided to group the Hospitallers into homogeneous language groups, the Tongues. Each Tongue included grand priories or priories, bailiwicks and commanderies.

The Tongues did not follow the pattern of nation states but rather the territorial and linguistic identities of Western Europe.

There were exceptions: the Poles and other Slavs (including the Czech lands), for example, belonged to the German Tongue even though they did not speak German.

At first there were seven Tongues in the Order: Provence, Auvergne, France, Italy, Aragon (Navarre), Germany and England. In 1492 Castile and Portugal separated from the Tongue of Aragon to form an eighth Tongue (Castile). Each Tongue had its own head, the pilier, who later held one of the high offices of the Order. On Rhodes and later on Malta every Tongue also had its own auberge, an inn used for lodging, meetings and meals, which, at least at first, had to be taken in common.

This internal organisation of the Knights of St. John was more or less complete by the middle of the 15th century and lasted until the end of the 18th century.

The loss of Malta in 1798 brought the old division into Tongues to an end. The Order began to reorganise, and after it settled in Rome in 1834 national associations were founded: the German knights were the first, in 1859, followed by the British in 1875 and the Italians in 1877. Today the members of the Order belong to the grand priories and national associations, the heirs of the tradition of the ancient Tongues, on five continents.

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/jmena-radu/.title: The names of the Order
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/jmena-radu/.description: From the Knights Hospitaller to the Knights of Malta: the names of the Order and its members over nine centuries.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/jmena-radu/.body:
Since its foundation, many different names have been used for the Order and its members.

This is partly because of the very long time the Order has existed, and partly because the knights were often forced to leave countries in which they had played a leading role.

The official name of the Order today is the Sovereign Military Hospitaller Order of St. John of Jerusalem of Rhodes and of Malta.

For legal, diplomatic and communication purposes shorter forms are often used: the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, the Sovereign Order of Malta or the Order of Malta.

At first the knights were called the Knights Hospitaller (or simply the Hospitallers), which describes their mission. They were also called the Knights of St. John (of Jerusalem), after the Order's patron, St. John the Baptist, and after Jerusalem, because of their presence in the Holy Land.

After the conquest of Rhodes in 1310 they became the Knights of Rhodes. In 1530 Emperor Charles V granted Malta to the knights, and since then the members of the Order have generally been known as the Knights of Malta.

To protect this heritage, the Order of Malta has registered its names and emblems in many countries.

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/velmistr/.title: The Grand Master
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/velmistr/.description: The office of the Grand Master of the Order of Malta, and His Most Eminent Highness Fra’ John T. Dunlap, the 81st Grand Master.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/velmistr/.body:
The Grand Master is elected for ten years by the Council Complete of State from among the professed knights.

Under the Constitution, as the religious superior and sovereign of the Order of Malta, he must devote himself fully to the development of the works of the Order and set an example of Christian life to all its members.

He holds the supreme authority. Together with the Sovereign Council the Grand Master issues legislative measures not contained in the Constitution, promulgates acts of government, manages the property of the Common Treasury, ratifies international agreements and convenes the Chapter General.

The states with which the Order has diplomatic relations accord the Grand Master the prerogatives, immunities and honours reserved for heads of state. The Grand Master bears the title of Most Eminent Highness, and the Holy Roman Church accords him the rank of a Cardinal.

The Grand Master resides in the Magistral Palace, the seat of the Order's government, in Rome.

His Most Eminent Highness the Prince and Grand Master Fra’ John T. Dunlap

Fra’ John T. Dunlap was born in Ottawa, Canada, in 1957. After studying at the University of Nice he graduated from the University of Ottawa and then took a law degree at the University of Western Ontario. John Cabot University in Rome awarded him an honorary doctorate in public service.

Fra’ John Dunlap is an attorney admitted to the New York State Bar and a barrister and solicitor of the Law Society of Ontario. In 1986 he joined the law firm Dunnington, Bartholow & Miller in New York and became a partner in 1993, specialising in corporate and immigration law. An internationally recognised lawyer, he has been legal counsel to the Permanent Observer Mission of the Holy See to the United Nations since 1997.

He came into contact with the Order of Malta and discovered his religious vocation in the mid-1980s while volunteering with patients suffering from AIDS and other diseases at the Cardinal Cooke Medical Center in Harlem, New York, where he volunteered every week for 30 years.

He was admitted to the Order of Malta in 1996 and took temporary vows as a Knight of Justice in 2004. In 2006 he was elected the first Regent (religious superior) of the Subpriory of Our Lady of Lourdes, based in New York. On 7 June 2008 he took solemn vows, becoming the first American member of the Order to be a professed knight. For more than ten years he served the Order as President of the Committee for the Protection of Names and Emblems and as its representative to the Alliance of the Orders of St. John.

In 2009 he was elected to the Sovereign Council for a five-year term, and the Chapter General re-elected him in 2014 and 2019. After the death of Fra’ Marco Luzzago he led the Order as Lieutenant of the Grand Master from June 2022. On 3 May 2023 the Council Complete of State elected him Grand Master.

/rad-a-jeho-instituce/velmistri/.title: Grand Masters of the Order
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/velmistri/.description: The Grand Masters of the Order of Malta from Blessed Gerard to Fra’ John T. Dunlap, with the Lieutenants.
/rad-a-jeho-instituce/velmistri/.body:
The first Grand Master: Blessed Gerard

c. 1040 – 1120

The founder and first Grand Master of the Order was born around 1040, probably in Scala, a village a few kilometres from Amalfi in southern Italy. In the second half of the 11th century he came to Jerusalem, where he began working in the hospital beside the church of St. Mary of the Latins, built by merchants from Amalfi to receive pilgrims and care for the sick.

Legend has it that in 1099, during the crusaders’ siege of Jerusalem, Blessed Gerard threw bread to them from the walls; when he was arrested for it, the bread miraculously turned to stone, and he escaped punishment by the city’s Muslim rulers.

To raise the standing of the institution he led, Blessed Gerard made it a religious order dedicated to St. John the Baptist. On 15 February 1113 Pope Paschal II officially recognised the religious community of the Hospitallers of St. John of Jerusalem. The papal document shows the role and importance of the founder and of the services offered to pilgrims and the poor in the hospital of Jerusalem. It also lists hospitals and hospices in France and Italy, showing that only a few decades after its foundation the Order of Blessed Gerard was not confined to the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem but already had a European dimension.

Blessed Gerard died in Jerusalem on 3 September 1120. His instructions and his example are the basis of the Order’s first written rule, issued by Fra’ Raymond du Puy, the second Grand Master, between 1145 and 1153.
The Catholic Church venerates him as Blessed; his memorial is on 13 October.

/ostatni/zasady-prijimani-daru/.title: Gift acceptance policy
/ostatni/zasady-prijimani-daru/.description: The principles governing how the Order of Malta and its entities accept gifts.
/ostatni/zasady-prijimani-daru/.body:
Translated from the Czech version of the Order’s policy (2021). The authoritative text is issued by the Grand Magistry.

Introduction

The Sovereign Military Hospitaller Order of St. John of Jerusalem of Rhodes and of Malta (“the Order”) raises funds from its members and from private and public donations. Sources of funding vary between countries, entities of the Order, types of project and circumstances. This policy sets out the main rules governing the Order’s approach to accepting gifts. It describes the steps expected to ensure that the Order is not exposed to undue reputational or compliance risk.

Scope

This policy applies to all entities of the Order of Malta and to volunteers acting on behalf of the Order, and to all other entities directly or indirectly controlled by the Order. It should be applied in accordance with local legal and regulatory requirements. Where a requirement of this policy is less strict than local law, entities should adopt the stricter local requirement.

Main rules

  • Entities of the Order should not accept gifts from donors where this would risk damaging the reputation of the Order or would otherwise harm its work.
  • In fundraising, entities of the Order should comply with all local laws and established good practice in the jurisdictions where they are registered or operate.
  • Entities of the Order should be very careful when allowing donors to publicise their connection with the Order, bearing in mind the donor’s possible motives for making that connection visible.

Expectations of entities

In the light of the rules above, all entities of the Order that raise funds are expected to follow a local gift acceptance policy. It should name the person or committee responsible for overseeing the acceptance of gifts (usually the board or the equivalent body of the entity) and, where appropriate, the delegation of decisions to executive management.

Local gift acceptance policies and procedures should:

  • Reflect the core values of the Order. Although every donor relationship should be assessed on its own merits, entities should not work with those whose funds come from sectors likely to conflict with Catholic teaching, such as arms or pornography.
  • Comply with local laws governing fundraising. All relevant staff should be familiar with these laws. Attention should also be paid to anti-money-laundering requirements and to the Order’s anti-money-laundering policy.
  • Set out a procedure for screening donors. It should be based both on an assessment of risk and on the value of the proposed gift, taking into account the cumulative effect of gifts from the same donor.
  • Require due diligence on donors proportionate to the value of the gift and the perceived risk. This may include, among other things, searching publicly available information, referring the matter to the Grand Magistry or using specialist research firms. Thresholds at which different procedures apply can help in choosing the most suitable approach.
  • Ensure that records are kept of prospective donors who have been screened. These records must be kept in accordance with the GDPR (or equivalent local law) and should document the reasons for the conclusion reached.
  • Set out a policy on anonymous gifts. Such gifts are prohibited or regulated (including maximum amounts) in some jurisdictions. Anonymous gifts should in any case be treated with particular caution and accepted only when the entity is satisfied that the gift comes from a lawful and acceptable source.

Gift acceptance policy (PDF, Czech)

/ostatni/zasady-boje-proti-prani-spinavy.title: Anti-money-laundering policy
/ostatni/zasady-boje-proti-prani-spinavy.description: The principles governing how the Order of Malta and its entities prevent money laundering and other financial crime.
/ostatni/zasady-boje-proti-prani-spinavy.body:
Translated from the Czech version of the Order’s policy (2021). The authoritative text is issued by the Grand Magistry.

Introduction

The Sovereign Military Hospitaller Order of St. John of Jerusalem of Rhodes and of Malta (“the Order”) has a worldwide presence and an international structure, and works in many areas, including places without conventional banking services and places in or near areas exposed to terrorist activity. The Order therefore faces the risk of becoming the target of attempts to use it to launder money that may have been obtained unlawfully.

This policy sets out the main rules governing the Order’s approach to preventing money laundering and other financial crime. It describes the steps expected to ensure that the Order is not exposed to undue reputational or compliance risk.

Scope

This policy applies to all entities of the Order of Malta and to volunteers acting on behalf of the Order, and to all other entities directly or indirectly controlled by the Order. It should be applied in accordance with local legal and regulatory requirements. Where a requirement of this policy is less strict than local law, entities should adopt the stricter local requirement.

Main rules

  • The Order should take all reasonable steps to prevent money laundering, terrorist financing and bribery.
  • In all financial transactions, entities of the Order should comply with all local laws and established good practice in the jurisdictions where they are registered or operate.

Expectations of entities

In the light of the rules above, all entities of the Order are expected to follow local policies and procedures on money laundering, bribery and terrorist financing. Their nature and structure will differ according to each entity’s work, but they should take account of all the applicable requirements below. The policies should name the person or committee responsible for overseeing financial control (usually the board or the equivalent body of the entity) and, where appropriate, the delegation of responsibility to executive management.

Entities should ensure that their local policies and procedures:

  • Allow full compliance with local law. Anti-money-laundering and anti-bribery laws differ widely between jurisdictions and are often highly prescriptive. It is essential that staff know their local obligations and are able to meet them.
  • Establish sound financial controls. For example, there should be payment approval thresholds under which, according to value and risk as determined by the entity’s governing body, a set number of approvals by staff of a given seniority is required.
  • Apply clear procedures and limits for cash payments. Although cash is unavoidable in some circumstances, it carries an inherently higher risk because it cannot be traced and can be stolen or lost. Sound procedures with a clear audit trail and authorisation protocols are therefore needed to limit and manage its use.
  • Show knowledge of sanctions regimes and ensure that no payments are made to prohibited individuals or organisations. This includes making sure that no payments are made to organisations that may be designated as terrorist.
  • Provide for the screening of prospective donors in line with the local gift acceptance policy. Reference should be made to the Order’s gift acceptance policy.
  • Make clear that bribery in any form is unacceptable. Staff should know their obligations: when a gift may amount to a bribe and how suspected bribery should be reported, both internally and to outside authorities. Accepting a bribe, or failing to report one, is a serious matter and may call for disciplinary action.
